GATE CSE Discrete Mathematics Previous Year Questions (Solved)

Question 1
NAT
| 2 Marks
Consider a function [latex]f : (0,1) \rightarrow \{0,1\}[/latex] defined as follows.

For a real number [latex]r \in (0,1)[/latex], [latex]f(r) = 1[/latex] if the second digit after the decimal point in [latex]r[/latex] is one of the four digits [latex]2, 3, 6,[/latex] and [latex]7[/latex]. Otherwise, [latex]f(r)[/latex] is equal to [latex]0[/latex].

The number of points in [latex](0,1)[/latex] at which [latex]f[/latex] is discontinuous is ______. (Answer in integer)
GATE CSE 2026 SET-2      Functions
Question 1 Explanation:
[latex]f(r)[/latex] depends only on the second digit after the decimal point of [latex]r[/latex]. So [latex](0,1)[/latex] is effectively divided into [latex]100[/latex] equal sub-intervals of length [latex]0.01[/latex] (one for each combination of the first two decimal digits), and [latex]f[/latex] is constant throughout each sub-interval, jumping only at the [latex]99[/latex] internal boundary points [latex]r=0.01,0.02,\ldots,0.99[/latex] (a discontinuity occurs at a boundary only if [latex]f[/latex]'s value actually changes across it, i.e. the second digit switches between the "special" set [latex]\{2,3,6,7\}[/latex] and the rest).

Within any fixed first digit, as the second digit cycles [latex]0,1,2,\ldots,9[/latex], the pattern of "special vs. non-special" is: N,N,S,S,N,N,S,S,N,N. Checking each of the [latex]9[/latex] consecutive transitions within this block ([latex]0|1,1|2,\ldots,8|9[/latex]): the value actually changes at [latex]1|2,\ 3|4,\ 5|6,[/latex] and [latex]7|8[/latex] (four changes), while it stays the same at the other five transitions (including the wrap from [latex]9[/latex] to the next first-digit's [latex]0[/latex], since both are non-special).

So each of the [latex]10[/latex] first-digit blocks contributes exactly [latex]4[/latex] genuine discontinuities, and the wrap-around boundaries between blocks never add any more (non-special to non-special). Total discontinuities [latex]=10\times4=40[/latex].

Answer: 40

Question 2
NAT
| 2 Marks
Suppose an unbiased coin is tossed [latex]6[/latex] times. Each coin toss is independent of all previous coin tosses. Let [latex]E_{1}[/latex] be the event that among the second, fourth, and sixth coin tosses, there are at least two heads. Let [latex]E_{2}[/latex] be the event that among the first, second, third, and fifth coin tosses, there are equal number of heads and tails.
The conditional probability [latex]{P}\left(E_{1} \mid E_{2}\right)[/latex] is equal to ________ (rounded off to one decimal place)
GATE CSE 2026 SET-2      Probability Theory
Question 2 Explanation:
Toss [latex]4[/latex] and toss [latex]6[/latex] don't appear at all in [latex]E_2[/latex]'s set [latex]\{1,2,3,5\}[/latex], so they remain completely independent, fair (unconditioned) coin flips regardless of [latex]E_2[/latex].

Toss [latex]2[/latex], however, is part of both [latex]E_1[/latex]'s set [latex]\{2,4,6\}[/latex] and [latex]E_2[/latex]'s set [latex]\{1,2,3,5\}[/latex]. Given [latex]E_2[/latex] (exactly [latex]2[/latex] heads among tosses [latex]1,2,3,5[/latex]), by symmetry among these [latex]4[/latex] fair, exchangeable coins, the conditional probability that any particular one of them (in particular, toss [latex]2[/latex]) is heads equals [latex]\dfrac{\binom{3}{1}}{\binom{4}{2}}=\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac12[/latex] — exactly the same as its unconditional probability. So conditioning on [latex]E_2[/latex] doesn't actually bias toss [latex]2[/latex]'s marginal chance of being heads at all.

So, given [latex]E_2[/latex], tosses [latex]2,4,[/latex] and [latex]6[/latex] behave exactly like [latex]3[/latex] independent fair coins. We need [latex]P(\text{at least }2\text{ heads out of }3\text{ fair coin flips})[/latex]:
[latex]P(X\ge2)=\binom{3}{2}(0.5)^3+\binom{3}{3}(0.5)^3=\dfrac{3}{8}+\dfrac{1}{8}=\dfrac{4}{8}=0.5[/latex].

Answer: 0.5

Question 3
MSQ
| 1 Mark
Let [latex]R[/latex] be a binary relation on the set [latex]\{1,2, \ldots, 10\}[/latex], where [latex](x, y) \in R[/latex] if the product of [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] is square of an integer. Which of the following properties is/are satisfied by [latex]R[/latex]?
A
Reflexive
B
Symmetric
C
Transitive
D
Antisymmetric
GATE CSE 2026 SET-2      Relation
Question 3 Explanation:
[latex](x,y)\in R[/latex] iff [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square.

- Reflexive: [latex]x\cdot x=x^2[/latex] is always a perfect square, so [latex](x,x)\in R[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex]. Holds.
- Symmetric: [latex]xy=yx[/latex], so if [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square then so is [latex]yx[/latex] (the same number). Holds.
- Transitive: Write each number as [latex]n=k^2\cdot s[/latex] where [latex]s[/latex] is its square-free part. Then [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square exactly when [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] have the same square-free part. This "same square-free part" relation is a genuine equivalence relation, so it is transitive: if [latex]x,y[/latex] share a square-free part and [latex]y,z[/latex] share the same square-free part, then [latex]x,z[/latex] do too, making [latex]xz[/latex] a perfect square. Holds.
- Antisymmetric: a counterexample: [latex]x=2,y=8[/latex] gives [latex]xy=16=4^2[/latex], so [latex](2,8)\in R[/latex] and (by symmetry) [latex](8,2)\in R[/latex] too, even though [latex]2\ne8[/latex]. Fails.

Answer: Reflexive, Symmetric, and Transitive all hold (R is an equivalence relation); Antisymmetric does not hold.

Question 4
MCQ
| 1 Mark
The probability density function [latex]f(x)[/latex] of a random variable [latex]X[/latex] which takes real values is

[latex] f(x)=\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2 \pi}} \exp \left(-\frac{x^{2}}{18}\right), \quad x \in(-\infty,+\infty) [/latex]

Which one of the following statements is correct about the random variable [latex]X[/latex] ?
A
[latex]X[/latex] is an exponential random variable
B
[latex]X[/latex] is a normal random variable
C
[latex]X[/latex] is a Poisson random variable
D
[latex]X[/latex] is a uniform random variable
GATE CSE 2026 SET-2      Probability Theory
Question 4 Explanation:
The given density [latex]f(x)=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\dfrac{x^2}{18}\right)[/latex] has exactly the form of the Gaussian/normal density [latex]f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\dfrac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)[/latex] with mean [latex]\mu=0[/latex] and, matching [latex]2\sigma^2=18\Rightarrow\sigma^2=9\Rightarrow\sigma=3[/latex] (consistent with the [latex]\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2\pi}}[/latex] normalizing constant).

This is the defining bell-curve density of a normal (Gaussian) random variable with mean [latex]0[/latex] and standard deviation [latex]3[/latex] — it doesn't match the forms of an exponential, Poisson (which is discrete, not even a continuous density), or uniform distribution.

Answer: X is a normal random variable

Question 5
MCQ
| 1 Mark
For two different persons [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex], the predicate [latex]M(x, y)[/latex] denotes that [latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex].
Consider the following statement.

There is a person who does not know anyone else, but that person is known by everyone else.

Which one of the following expressions represents the above statement?
A
[latex](\exists y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
B
[latex](\forall y)(\exists x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
C
[latex](\exists y)(\exists x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
D
[latex](\forall y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
GATE CSE 2026 SET-2      Propositional Logic
Question 5 Explanation:
We need to translate: "There is a person [latex]y[/latex] such that [latex]y[/latex] doesn't know anyone else, but everyone else knows [latex]y[/latex]."

- "There is a person [latex]y[/latex]" → [latex](\exists y)[/latex].
- "for every other person [latex]x[/latex] ([latex]x\ne y[/latex])" → [latex](\forall x)(x\ne y\rightarrow\ldots)[/latex].
- "[latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex]" (everyone else knows this person) → [latex]M(x,y)[/latex].
- "[latex]y[/latex] does not know [latex]x[/latex]" (this person doesn't know anyone else) → [latex]\neg M(y,x)[/latex].

Combining: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)\big((x\ne y)\rightarrow(M(x,y)\wedge\neg M(y,x))\big)[/latex] — there exists such a special person [latex]y[/latex], and for every other person [latex]x[/latex], [latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex] but [latex]y[/latex] does not know [latex]x[/latex].

The other options either use [latex]\forall y[/latex] (wrongly requiring every person to have this property, instead of just one special person), or use [latex]\exists x[/latex] (existentially quantifying [latex]x[/latex] instead of requiring it for every other person), which don't match the intended meaning.

Answer: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)\left((x\neq y)\rightarrow(M(x,y)\wedge\neg M(y,x))\right)[/latex]

GATE CSE Discrete Mathematics Previous Year Questions (Solved)

Discrete Mathematics is one of the most important and scoring subjects in GATE CSE. It forms the mathematical foundation for subjects like Algorithms, Theory of Computation, Graph Theory, and Computer Networks.

On this page, you can practice GATE CSE Discrete Mathematics previous year questions topic-wise with detailed step-by-step solutions designed exactly as per the GATE pattern.

Topics Covered in Discrete Mathematics

  • Propositional Logic
  • Set Theory
  • Relation
  • Functions
  • Lattice
  • Group Theory
  • Graph Theory
  • Planar Graph
  • Combination
  • Probability Theory
  • Recurrence

Why Discrete Mathematics is Important for GATE?

Discrete Mathematics usually contributes 8–12 marks in GATE CSE. It is highly conceptual and logical, making it one of the most scoring areas if prepared properly.

Many algorithmic and theoretical subjects directly depend on Discrete Mathematics. Strong fundamentals here will automatically improve your performance in:

  • Algorithms
  • Theory of Computation
  • Compiler Design
  • Computer Networks

Important Areas to Focus

1. Propositional Logic
Truth tables, logical equivalence, normal forms (CNF, DNF), and inference rules are frequently asked.

2. Graph Theory & Planar Graph
Degree properties, Euler’s formula, connectivity, trees, spanning trees, and graph coloring are common question areas.

3. Probability Theory & Combination
Conditional probability, Bayes theorem, permutations, combinations, and counting principles are highly scoring.

4. Recurrence
Solving recurrence relations using substitution method and characteristic equation is essential for GATE.

5. Relations, Functions & Set Theory
Equivalence relations, partial orders, injective/surjective functions and set identities are repeatedly tested concepts.

How to Prepare Discrete Mathematics for GATE 2026?

  • Solve topic-wise previous year questions.
  • Practice logical reasoning problems daily.
  • Memorize important formulas and theorems.
  • Revise Graph Theory and Probability regularly.

For official exam updates and syllabus details, refer to the GATE 2026 Official Website.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

1. How many marks are expected from Discrete Mathematics in GATE?

Typically 8–12 marks are asked every year.

2. Is Discrete Mathematics difficult for GATE CSE?

It is logical and conceptual but highly scoring if fundamentals are strong.

3. Which topics are most important in Discrete Mathematics?

Graph Theory, Probability Theory, Propositional Logic, and Recurrence are very important.

4. Should I solve PYQs for Discrete Mathematics?

Yes, previous year questions are essential because similar concepts are frequently repeated.
